g9-economics-ue6-t1.overview: Money is whatever people generally accept in payment for goods and services and in the repayment of debts. This lesson defines money, explains why social convention makes it accepted, and lists the five criteria a commodity must meet to serve as money.
objectives: Define money as anything generally accepted in payment for goods, services and the repayment of debts
Explain why each person accepts money on the confidence that others will accept it too
Identify the criteria a commodity must satisfy to be accepted as money
Distinguish the economist's meaning of money from the everyday use of the word for currency
Explain money's acceptance as a social convention established through legal or other means
g9-economics-ue6-t1.simple: Money is anything that people generally accept when paying for goods and services or when repaying debts. In everyday speech people say money and mean currency, such as birr notes and coins. To an economist, money is any good widely used and accepted in transactions that move goods and services from one person to another. It is a commodity accepted by common consent as a medium of economic exchange. Each person accepts money because he or she is confident that others will accept it in turn, so money's value rests on social convention, which may be established through legal or other means. For a commodity to serve as money it must be standardized, widely acceptable, divisible, portable and durable.
g9-economics-ue6-t1.detailed:
The economist's definition. Economists define money as anything generally accepted in payment for goods or services or in the repayment of debts. When most people talk about money, however, they are talking about currency, the notes and coins in hand. The textbook imagines a person shouting for your money and your life: you would quickly hand over all your currency rather than risk your life, and you would not stop to ask what exactly is meant by money. The economist uses a broader idea than the ordinary one.

Money as a medium of economic exchange. Money is any good that is widely used and accepted in transactions involving the transfer of goods and services from one person to another. It is a commodity accepted by general consent as a medium of economic exchange. It serves as the medium for expressing prices and values; as currency, it circulates anonymously from person to person and country to country, facilitating trade and serving as the primary measure of wealth.

The essential characteristic. An essential characteristic of money is that it is immediately exchangeable for all kinds of marketable assets, such as goods and services, real estate, or whatever else. Each person accepts money as a means of payment because he or she is confident that others will accept it as payment from him or her. The social convention behind acceptance could be established through legal or other means, and money is accepted customarily without any special test of its quality or quantity.

Where money originates. Generally speaking, money is an economic unit that functions as a generally recognized medium of exchange for transactional purposes in an economy. It originates in the form of a commodity, having a physical property that market participants can adopt as a medium of exchange. All other commodities are then expressed and valued in terms of the commodity regarded as money.

Criteria for a commodity to be accepted as money. A commodity must meet five criteria. Standardization: it must be easily standardized, making it simple to ascertain its value. Acceptability: it must be widely accepted as a medium of exchange. Divisibility: it must be divisible so that it is easy to make change. Portability: it must be easy to carry. Durability: it should not degrade quickly.

Reading the criteria on a birr note. A birr note passes all five tests: its denominations are standardized so its value is certain; it is accepted everywhere in Ethiopia; it comes in different values so change can be made; it is light and easy to carry; and it is durable enough to pass through thousands of transactions. A commodity such as a live ox fails several tests at once: it is hard to carry, it cannot be cut for change without losing its value, and its quality must be tested every time it changes hands.

workedExamples.problem: A shopkeeper in Dessie takes a 100 birr note from a stranger without testing its quality or counting its weight. Which feature of money does this show?
workedExamples.given: The note is accepted immediately, without any special test of quality or quantity.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: money is accepted customarily because of general consent and wide acceptability.
workedExamples.substitution: The shopkeeper is confident other shops will accept the same note later, so the note meets the acceptability criterion.
workedExamples.calculation: Apply the checklist: standardized value, widely accepted, divisible, portable, durable; the decisive point here is general acceptability by social convention.
workedExamples.answer: Acceptability based on social convention: money is accepted without any special test of quality or quantity.

workedExamples.problem: A family considers using a live cow as money for the weekly market. Use the five criteria to judge whether it can serve.
workedExamples.given: A cow has high value but is heavy, indivisible for change making, and its health must be inspected by each buyer.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a commodity must be standardized, acceptable, divisible, portable and durable,
workedExamples.substitution: Test each criterion: not portable for small purchases, not divisible, quality must be tested each time.
workedExamples.calculation: It fails portability and divisibility outright, and lack of standardization means every exchange needs a special test.
workedExamples.answer: No. The cow fails portability, divisibility and standardization, so it cannot serve as money.

workedExamples.problem: A student argues that only notes and coins printed by the National Bank of Ethiopia are money. Judge the claim using the economist's definition.
workedExamples.given: The definition of money is anything generally accepted in payment for goods, services or debts.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the test is general acceptance in exchange, not the issuer or material.
workedExamples.substitution: In Ethiopian history a bar of salt (amole) was widely accepted in exchange before modern notes existed.
workedExamples.calculation: Since amole was generally accepted in payment, it satisfied the definition of money even though no bank issued it.
workedExamples.answer: The claim is wrong: any commodity accepted by general consent in exchange, such as amole, is money.

workedExamples.problem: Why does a trader in Addis Ababa accept a paper birr note that is almost worthless as paper? Explain the mechanism.
workedExamples.given: The note's material value is far below its face value.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: each person accepts money because he or she is confident others will accept it as payment in turn.
workedExamples.substitution: The trader's confidence rests on a social convention reinforced by the legal tender status of the currency.
workedExamples.calculation: The acceptance chain holds because every buyer and seller expects the next one to accept the note.
workedExamples.answer: Because of confidence in general acceptance: the social convention, backed by law, makes paper money immediate exchangeable purchasing power.

commonMistakes: Defining money narrowly as only coins or notes, forgetting that any generally accepted commodity can be money.
Confusing money with income or wealth, when the definition concerns what is accepted in exchange.
Believing a commodity becomes money because of its material worth rather than general consent.
Listing criteria such as portability and divisibility as optional conveniences rather than requirements.
Thinking acceptance of money requires a special test of quality and quantity each time.
Forgetting that durability matters because money changes hands thousands of times before it wears out.
applications: Birr notes are accepted anywhere in Ethiopia without checking who spent them before, because acceptance is customary.
Explaining why a bar of salt (amole) could circulate as money helps you test any commodity against the five criteria.
A cashier making change for a 100 birr note relies on divisibility of the currency.
Carrying a light wallet instead of heavy commodities to market shows the value of portability.
The legal tender status of the birr shows how social convention can be supported by law.
Judging whether a shop's store credit coupons could become money is an exercise in checking acceptability.
g9-economics-ue6-t1.summary: Money is anything generally accepted in payment for goods and services or in the repayment of debts, a commodity accepted by general consent as a medium of economic exchange. Each person accepts it on the confidence that others will accept it too, a social convention established through legal or other means. To serve as money a commodity must be standardized, widely acceptable, divisible, portable and durable.

g9-economics-ue6-t2.overview: Money did not always exist: exchange grew out of self-sufficiency, passed through barter and then evolved through commodity money, paper currency, fiat money, checks and electronic payments. Ethiopia travelled its own version of this road, from Axumite coins and amole salt to the birr of 1945.
objectives: Trace how self-sufficient households gave way to exchange and to the barter system
Define barter and describe the barter economy
Explain the limitations of barter, including the lack of double coincidence of wants
Sequence the evolution of the payments system from commodity money to electronic means of payment
Describe the history of money in Ethiopia, from Axumite coins to the birr
g9-economics-ue6-t2.simple: Before money existed, people were self-sufficient, producing everything they needed themselves. As needs grew through learning by doing and family formation, self-sufficiency ended and exchange began, first as barter, the direct exchange of goods for goods. Barter was clumsy: it required a double coincidence of wants, had no common measure of value, and made indivisible goods, stored wealth and future payments hard to handle. To fix these problems money evolved through stages: commodity money such as salt, then light paper currency, then fiat money decreed as legal tender, then checks, and finally electronic payments. Ethiopia followed this path too: Axumite coins, salt bars (amole) and the Maria Theresa thaler came before Menelik II's coins and the birr of 1945.
g9-economics-ue6-t2.detailed:
From self-sufficiency to exchange. Life among ancient humans was simple: everybody produced whatever the individual required, hunting and gathering, making clothing and building a dwelling, so economic activities were confined to production and consumption. In the course of time, learning by doing, the formation of families and rising needs made it impossible for each person to produce everything alone. Self-sufficiency came to an end and the process of exchange started.

Barter and its economy. Initially the exchange was direct, goods for goods, an exchange known as barter. Under the barter system an individual produces more than he or she can consume in order to exchange the surplus with another person for something needed in return. The economy based upon this system of exchange is called the barter economy.

Limitations of the barter system. Barter carries serious difficulties. Lack of double coincidence of wants is the most important problem: a person with a surplus must find another person who not only wants that commodity but also has something acceptable to offer in exchange. Lack of a common measure of value makes the terms of trade hard to settle, for example deciding what proportion of wheat equals a sheep. Indivisibility of commodities makes some exchanges unthinkable, such as exchanging a horse for a pair of shoes, since cutting the horse destroys its value. Difficulty in storing and transferring wealth arises because goods like rice, wheat, cattle and skins lose value over time and cost much to transport. Difficulty in deferred payments appears because goods lack stable prices, quality standards and general acceptability, so future payments in goods are unreliable.

Commodity money, paper currency and fiat money. When barter was replaced by the monetary system, primitive money was first used as commodity money, the particular commodity chosen depending on the location and economic development of the community. The problem with payment systems based on commodity money is that such money is very heavy and hard to transport. The next step was paper currency, pieces of paper that function as a medium of exchange, initially a promise convertible into coins or precious metal. In most countries currency then evolved into fiat money, paper currency decreed by governments as legal tender, meaning it must legally be accepted in payment of debts, but not convertible into coins or precious metal. Paper is much lighter, but it is accepted only if people trust the issuing authorities and if printing is advanced enough that counterfeiting is extremely difficult.

Checks. Paper currency and coins are easily stolen and expensive to transport in bulk. Modern banking answered with the check: a person with a checking account writes checks for payments and the holder cashes the check at the bank. Checks are payable on demand, allowing transactions without carrying large amounts of currency; they can be written for any amount up to the account balance; they reduce transportation costs, greatly reduce loss from theft, and provide convenient receipts for purchases.

Electronic means of payment. With computers and advanced telecommunications, all paperwork could be eliminated by converting completely to the electronic means of payment (EMOP), in which all payments are made using electronic telecommunications. Examples of e-money at this stage include visa cards and credit cards.

Money in Ethiopian history. From the third century A.D., during the reign of King Endybis and Aphilas, the Axumite kingdom used its own coins for internal and external trade; after the fall of the kingdom the coins disappeared and commodities such as a bar of salt (amole), cloth and beads served as money, with salt the most important and widespread. The Maria Theresa Thaler, first minted in Vienna in 1751 to commemorate the coronation of Maria Theresa as empress of Austria, entered Ethiopia through traders between the late 18th and early 19th century; it was never legal currency in Austria itself, yet served as a medium of exchange in Ethiopia until 1945. Emperor Menelik II minted the first national coin in 1893, replaced in July 1933 by coins bearing the image of Emperor Haileselassie. Paper money was first issued by the Bank of Abyssinia in 1914 but failed to gain acceptance because people were familiar only with metallic coins; the Bank of Ethiopia issued paper again in 1932, 100 percent backed by gold deposits, serving alongside salt bars and the Maria Theresa until the Italian occupation in 1936. After liberation in 1941 the country had no national currency, so foreign currencies circulated, including the Italian Lire, the Maria Theresa Dollar, the East African Shilling, the Indian Rupee and the Egyptian Pound. In July 1945 the Ethiopian government issued the national currency, the Birr, and with the growth of the banking system checks also came into use.

keyTerms.def: The direct exchange of goods for goods without the mediation of money; the economy built on it is called a barter economy.
The requirement that two traders each want exactly what the other offers; the most important problem of barter.
Primitive money in the form of a useful commodity, such as salt bars, whose choice depended on the community's location and development.
Paper currency decreed by governments as legal tender but not convertible into coins or precious metal.
Money that legally must be accepted as payment for debts.
A written order payable on demand that transfers money from a checking account at a bank.
Electronic means of payment, in which all payments are made using electronic telecommunications.
A bar of salt that served as the most popular commodity money in Ethiopia before the birr.

workedExamples.problem: A farmer wants to trade a sheep for wheat without money. Which limitation of barter does he face first in arranging the trade?
workedExamples.given: The farmer needs wheat; wheat growers may or may not want sheep.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: barter requires a double coincidence of wants.
workedExamples.substitution: The farmer must find a wheat grower who wants a sheep at the same time and has surplus wheat to offer.
workedExamples.calculation: Since such a partner is rare, the search itself is the first obstacle, before any price is agreed.
workedExamples.answer: Lack of double coincidence of wants, the most important limitation of the barter system.

workedExamples.problem: Someone offers to exchange a horse for a single pair of shoes. Explain why this exchange is unthinkable under barter.
workedExamples.given: The horse is indivisible and much more valuable than the shoes.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: indivisibility of commodities obstructs exchanges of unequal value.
workedExamples.substitution: Paying with part of the horse on the basis of the exchange ratio destroys the horse's identity and value.
workedExamples.calculation: Neither trader can give a fraction of a horse, so the ratio cannot be settled.
workedExamples.answer: Indivisibility of commodities prevents the exchange from taking place in any fair proportion.

workedExamples.problem: Order the stages of the payments system the world has passed through, and say which problem each stage removed.
workedExamples.given: Stages: barter, commodity money, paper currency, fiat money, checks, electronic payment.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: each stage reduces transaction and transportation costs further.
workedExamples.substitution: Commodity money answered the double coincidence problem; paper currency eased the weight of metal; fiat money freed currency from convertibility; checks cut the cost of carrying cash; electronic payment removes paperwork.
workedExamples.calculation: Match each problem to its stage and the chain is complete.
workedExamples.answer: Barter, commodity money, paper currency, fiat money, checks, electronic means of payment; each stage cuts transport, storage and transaction costs.

workedExamples.problem: Paper money issued in 1914 by the Bank of Abyssinia failed to gain acceptance. Diagnose the reason using the conditions for successful currency.
workedExamples.given: Fiat paper is accepted only if there is trust in the issuing authority and printing is hard to counterfeit.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: paper currency must be trusted and recognizable as money.
workedExamples.substitution: In 1914 most Ethiopian society was familiar only with metallic coins, so paper lacked general acceptability.
workedExamples.calculation: The acceptability criterion failed because users were not accustomed to paper as money.
workedExamples.answer: Lack of general acceptability: people trusted metal coins, not unfamiliar paper, so the 1914 notes could not circulate widely.

commonMistakes: Confusing barter with trade in general; barter is specifically the direct exchange of goods for goods.
Reporting the double coincidence of wants as a minor problem, when the textbook calls it the most important.
Believing commodity money always meant coins; salt bars, cloth and beads also served as money.
Thinking fiat money is convertible into precious metal; fiat money is not convertible into coins or precious metal.
Forgetting that Maria Theresa was never legal currency in its country of origin, Austria.
Assuming the birr existed from the time of Menelik II; the birr was issued in July 1945.
Treating checks as a form of electronic money; checks came before electronic payments.
applications: Explaining why farmers in a rural market once settled trades in amole rather than guess-work barter.
Tracing from Axumite coins through the Maria Theresa to the birr helps you discuss Ethiopia's monetary independence.
Comparing transport costs shows why a merchant hauling coins preferred opening a checking account to carrying cash.
The trust condition on paper currency explains why counterfeit-poor printing matters to a country.
Reading the 1945 introduction of the birr clarifies why 1941-1945 saw many foreign currencies circulating.
Judging whether a modern voucher could be money repeats the analysis the textbook applies to amole.
g9-economics-ue6-t2.summary: Exchange grew when self-sufficiency ended, and early exchange was barter, the direct swap of goods for goods. Barter failed through the double coincidence of wants, no common measure of value, indivisibility, and the difficulty of storing, transferring and deferring wealth, so money evolved from commodity money through paper currency, fiat money, checks and electronic payment. Ethiopia's own history ran from Axumite coins and salt bars through Maria Theresa thalers, Menelik II's coins of 1893 and gold-backed notes of 1932 to the birr issued in July 1945.

g9-economics-ue6-t3.overview: Every function money performs helps the economy run smoothly. This lesson explains the four basic functions of money: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value, and standard of deferred payments, and introduces liquidity as the reason people still hold money.
objectives: Explain the medium of exchange function and how it lowers transaction costs
Show how money as a unit of account enables orderly pricing and rational economic calculation
Describe money as a store of value and define liquidity
Explain money as a standard of deferred payments and its role in transferring resources
Compare money with other assets, such as stocks, bonds and houses, as stores of value
g9-economics-ue6-t3.simple: In every society money performs four basic functions. Most basically it is a medium of exchange: goods and services are paid for with currency or checks instead of being swapped directly, which removes the wasted searching time economists call transaction cost. Money is also a unit of account, the single unit, like the birr, in which every value is measured and expressed, just as weight is measured in kilograms. As a store of value it keeps purchasing power from the time income is received until it is spent; money is not unique in this, but it wins on liquidity, the ease and speed of converting an asset into a medium of exchange. Finally, as a standard of deferred payments, money buys now and pays later, moving spending power from savers to borrowers and investment.
g9-economics-ue6-t3.detailed:
Four functions in every society. In every society money performs four basic functions: medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payments. All of them play significant roles in the operation of the economy.

Money as a medium of exchange. The most basic function of money is to serve as a medium of exchange. In almost all market transactions, money in the form of currency or checks is used to pay for goods and services. Money has no power to satisfy human wants directly, but it has the power to purchase things that have utility and do satisfy wants. Using money as a medium of exchange promotes economic efficiency by eliminating the time spent exchanging goods and services. The time spent trying to exchange goods or a service is called the transaction cost. In a barter economy transaction costs are high because people must satisfy a double coincidence of wants, finding someone who has what they want and who also wants what they have. Money is therefore a lubricant that lets the economy run more smoothly by lowering transaction costs and encouraging specialization and the division of labour.

Money as a unit of account. The second role of money is to provide a unit of account, used to measure value in the economy; we measure the value of goods and services in terms of money just as we measure weight in pounds or distance in miles. Picture shopping in a supermarket with a thousand different items: to compare prices, every price tag would have to list up to 999 different exchange ratios, and the time spent reading them would be a very high transaction cost. Money units solve the problem because they serve as the measuring unit in which all values are expressed. This enables an orderly pricing system, which is essential for rational economic calculation and choice and for transmitting economic information among individuals.

Money as a store of value. Money also functions as a store of value, a repository of purchasing power over time. A store of value is used to save purchasing power from the time income is received until it is spent, which matters because most of us do not want to spend our income the moment it arrives. Money is not unique as a store of value: money, stocks, bonds, land, houses, art and jewellery can all store wealth, and many such assets have advantages over money, often paying the owner a higher interest rate, maintaining price value, or providing a service as a house does.

Why people still hold money: liquidity. If other assets are more desirable stores of value, why do people hold money at all? The answer is the economic concept of liquidity, the relative ease and speed with which an asset can be converted into a medium of exchange. Money is perfectly liquid, while converting a house means finding a buyer first, so holding some wealth as money buys convenience and readiness.

Money as a standard of deferred payments. Money lets you buy now and pay later, or lend now and collect later. When people save money, that money can be borrowed and channeled into investment. It is the deferred payment function of money that permits this transfer of spending power from savers (earners) to borrowers (spenders), and it permits the easy transfer of resources out of less desired, less productive and less profitable uses into more desired, more productive and more profitable uses.

keyTerms.def: Money's most basic function: the instrument used to pay for goods and services.

A repository of purchasing power over time, saving value from the receipt of income until it is spent.
The relative ease and speed with which an asset can be converted into a medium of exchange.
The function that lets people buy now and pay later, or lend now and collect later.
The specialization of workers in separate tasks, which money encourages by lowering transaction costs.
The textbook's image for money: it lets the economy run more smoothly.

g9-economics-ue6-t3.summary: Money performs four basic functions in every society: it is a medium of exchange that pays for goods and services and lowers transaction costs; a unit of account that lets every value be measured and compared; a store of value that holds purchasing power between income and expenditure; and a standard of deferred payments that lets people buy now and pay later, moving resources from savers to borrowers and into more productive uses. Money is not the only store of value, but it is the most liquid asset.

g9-economics-ue6-t4.overview: Why do people hold money instead of interest-earning assets, and how much money is there to hold? This lesson contrasts the old transaction-based view of money demand with Keynes' liquidity preference and its three motives, then defines the money supply and its components.
objectives: Contrast the old transaction-based idea of the demand for money with the modern Keynesian view
Explain the transaction motive, distinguishing the income motive from the business motive
Explain the precautionary and speculative motives for holding money
Identify the components that constitute the supply of money in a country
Explain why currency dominates in developing countries and how credit control policies affect the money supply
g9-economics-ue6-t4.simple: How much money do people want to hold, and how much money exists? The old view said money is demanded to complete business transactions, so demand rises in a boom and falls when trade is quiet. John Maynard Keynes gave the modern view: liquidity preference, the demand for money to hold. People hold money for three motives: transactions, to bridge the gap between receiving income and daily spending; precaution, to cover unforeseen contingencies such as sickness, accidents and unemployment; and speculation, to hold liquid resources and profit from future changes in interest rates. The money supply is the sum total of all forms of money held by the community at any given moment: metallic money or coins, currency notes and chequable bank deposits, composed broadly of currency with the public and deposit money with the public.
g9-economics-ue6-t4.detailed:
The old and modern ideas of money demand. The old idea was that money was demanded to complete business transactions, so the demand for money depended on the volume of trade: it increased during a boom and decreased during a depression or lull in trade. The modern idea was put forward by John Maynard Keynes, the famous English economist, the founder of what is called Keynesian Economics. According to Keynes, the demand for money, which he called liquidity preference, means the demand for money to hold. People want money for three main reasons: the transactional motive, the precautionary motive and the speculative motive.

The transaction motive. This motive can be seen from two perspectives. The income motive belongs to consumers: individuals hold cash to bridge the interval between the receipt of income and its expenditure. Most people receive income weekly or monthly while expenditure is day by day, so a certain amount of money is kept on hand for current payments; the amount depends on the size of the income, the interval at which income is received, and the methods of payment current in the locality. The business motive belongs to businessmen and entrepreneurs, who keep part of their resources in ready cash to pay for raw materials and transport, wages and salaries, and all other current expenses. The money held under the business motive depends to a very large extent on the turnover, the volume of trade of the firm: the larger the turnover, the greater the amount of money needed.

The precautionary motive. The precautionary motive is the desire to hold cash balances for unforeseen contingencies. People hold money to provide for the risk of unemployment, sickness, accidents and other uncertain losses. The amount held depends on the nature of the individual and on the conditions in which he or she lives.

The speculative motive. The speculative motive relates to the desire to hold one's resources in liquid form in order to take advantage of market movements, regarding future changes in the rate of interest or bond prices. Money held under this motive serves as a store of value, just as money held under the precautionary motive does, but it is a store of money meant for a different purpose. The amounts required under all the motives together constitute the demand for money.

The supply of money. Just as the demand for money is the demand for money to hold, the supply of money means the supply of money to hold. Money must always be held by someone, otherwise it cannot exist. The supply of money therefore means the sum total of all the forms of money held by a community at any given moment. It consists of metallic money or coins, currency notes issued by the currency authority of the country, whether the central bank or the government, and chequable bank deposits. In old times coins formed the bulk of the money supply; later currency notes eclipsed metallic currency, and now bank deposits in current accounts withdrawable by cheques have overwhelmed all other forms of money.

Composing the money supply. Broadly speaking, the money supply is composed of two main elements: currency with the public, and deposit money with the public. To arrive at the total currency with the public, we add currency notes in circulation, the circulation of birr notes and coins, and the circulation of small coins, and from the total we deduct cash in hand with banks. The bulk of the currency in the hands of the public is in the form of currency notes issued by the National Bank of Ethiopia.

Currency dominance and credit control. Besides currency, the public's money includes deposit money, the bank balances held in current accounts. Currency rather than bank deposits has a dominant position in developing countries because the majority of commercial transactions are conducted in cash as a medium of exchange, rather than through cheques as in advanced countries. Thus the supply of money in a country, by and large, depends on the credit control policies pursued by the banking system of the country.

workedExamples.problem: A community holds currency notes worth 500 million birr, birr coins 60 million, small coins 40 million, while banks hold 100 million of that total in their vaults. Compute currency with the public.

workedExamples.formula: Principle: precautionary motive covers unforeseen contingencies; speculative motive takes advantage of future interest or bond price changes.
workedExamples.substitution: Illness risk is an unforeseen contingency; buying on rate expectations is speculation.
workedExamples.calculation: Match each purpose to its motive.
workedExamples.answer: The teacher holds under the precautionary motive; the friend holds under the speculative motive.

commonMistakes: Attributing the three motives to the old view rather than to Keynes' modern idea of liquidity preference.
Confusing the transaction motive with the precautionary motive; one covers planned spending, the other unforeseen contingencies.
Thinking the business motive depends on personal income, when it depends on the firm's turnover.
Defining money supply as only currency notes, forgetting chequable bank deposits.
Forgetting to deduct cash in hand with banks when computing currency with the public.
Believing the money supply depends on the supply of goods rather than on the banking system's credit control policies.
Assuming deposit money dominates everywhere; currency dominates in developing countries.

A textile trader in Merkato increasing cash stocks as sales grow is following the business motive.

The National Bank of Ethiopia's decisions on currency notes show how the money supply is managed.
Watching whether a shop accepts deposits or only cash shows the currency dominance of developing countries.
g9-economics-ue6-t4.summary: The old view tied money demand to the volume of trade, but Keynes explained the demand for money as liquidity preference, money held under three motives: transaction (income motive and business motive), precaution (unforeseen contingencies) and speculation (profit from future interest rate changes). The supply of money is the sum total of all forms of money held by the community, composed of currency with the public and deposit money with the public, its bulk comprising currency notes issued by the National Bank of Ethiopia. The money supply depends largely on the credit control policies of the banking system.

g9-economics-ue6-t5.overview: Electronic money stores monetary value on a technical device and moves it without paper. This lesson defines e-money, describes its forms, such as cards, ATMs and electronic fund transfer, and weighs its advantages against its disadvantages.
objectives: Define electronic money as an electronic store of monetary value on a technical device
Describe the ways payments are performed in systems of e-money, including cards and ATMs
Explain electronic fund transfer and the role of cards, codes and PINs in accessing accounts
List the advantages of e-money
Identify the disadvantages and risks of e-money
g9-economics-ue6-t5.simple: Electronic money (e-money) is an electronic store of monetary value on a technical device that may be used widely for making payments. Payments run through debit cards, prepaid cards and credit cards at point of sale terminals, through 24-hour cash from automated teller machines (ATMs) and through direct deposit of pay checks into bank accounts. E-money is also called electronic fund transfer (EFT): computers and electronic technology replace checks and paper transactions, and cards, codes and personal identification numbers (PINs) let you, or those you authorize, access your account. In Ethiopia, ATMs are electronic terminals that let you bank almost any time. E-money moves money quickly and carries large sums without physical burden, but it brings cybercrime, money laundering risks and a need for training and hardware.
g9-economics-ue6-t5.detailed:
What electronic money is. Electronic money is an electronic store of monetary value on a technical device that may be used widely for making payments. Payments can be performed in a number of ways, such as debit cards, prepaid cards and credit cards, which make paying at point of sale terminals quick and simple.

Everyday meanings. For many people, electronic money means 24-hour access to cash through an automated teller machine (ATM), or the direct deposit of paychecks into checking or savings accounts. Broadly speaking, electronic money involves many different types of transactions, rights and responsibilities, and sometimes fees.

Electronic fund transfer (EFT). Electronic money is also known as electronic fund transfer, which uses computers and electronic technology in place of checks and other paper transactions. EFT is initiated through devices like cards or codes that let you, or those you authorize, access your account. Many financial institutions use ATM or debit cards and personal identification numbers (PINs) for this purpose; some people use other debit cards that require a signature or a scan. In the Ethiopian context, ATMs are electronic terminals that let you bank almost any time.

Advantages of e-money. The textbook lists four: the ability to move money quickly; better record keeping; global money transfers; and the ability to move large sums of money without any physical burden. Together these cut the transport and paperwork problems that worried earlier stages of the payments system.

Disadvantages of e-money. The same technology creates new risks: cybercrime and new digital forms of money laundering; users must have a minimum level of training and knowledge, especially for more complicated forms of electronic transfer; some types of e-money, most notably cryptocurrencies, are closely linked to criminal activity; and both hardware and software are required to perform transfers of electronic cash. So the gains of speed and scale come with security, skill and equipment requirements.

Reading the balance of advantage. Compare e-money with the drawbacks that pushed earlier payments systems forward: coins and currency were easily stolen and expensive to transport in bulk, while checks still needed paperwork. E-money answers both, moving sums of any size at almost no physical cost while keeping digital records, which explains why banks and telecom payment services keep expanding card, ATM and digital transfer facilities.

Listing only advantages of e-money and ignoring cybercrime, money laundering and the training requirement.
Believing e-money needs no equipment, when both hardware and software are required.
Assuming fund transfers always leave no records, when better recordkeeping is an advantage of e-money.
Forgetting that some forms of e-money, notably cryptocurrencies, are linked to criminal activity.

g9-economics-ue6-t6.overview: This lesson consolidates Unit 6: what money is and why social convention makes it accepted, how money evolved from barter to electronic payment including Ethiopia's own history, the four functions money performs, the demand for and supply of money, and the promises and risks of e-money.
objectives: Restate the definition of money and the criteria a commodity must meet to serve as money
Recall the stages of the payments system and the milestones of Ethiopian monetary history
Match each situation to the function of money it illustrates
Classify demands for money under Keynes' three motives and identify the components of money supply
Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of electronic money
g9-economics-ue6-t6.simple: Money is anything generally accepted in payment for goods and services or in the repayment of debts, accepted by general consent because each person is confident others will accept it too. It arose because barter, the direct exchange of goods for goods, suffered from the double coincidence of wants, the lack of a common measure of value, indivisibility, and the difficulty of storing, transferring and deferring wealth. Money evolved from commodity money through paper currency, fiat money, checks and electronic payment; in Ethiopia this ran from Axumite coins and amole salt through the Maria Theresa thaler, Menelik II's coins and the 1945 birr. Money's four functions are medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payments. Keynes explained holding money through transaction, precautionary and speculative motives, and the money supply consists of currency with the public and deposit money.
g9-economics-ue6-t6.detailed:
Definition and criteria. Money is anything generally accepted in payment for goods or services or in the repayment of debts; in everyday speech it means currency, such as birr notes and coins. As a commodity accepted by general consent, money is immediately exchangeable for all kinds of marketable assets and circulates anonymously from person to person and country to country. A commodity must meet five criteria to serve as money: standardization, acceptability, divisibility, portability and durability.

Evolution of money. Exchange began when self-sufficiency ended, and the first exchange was barter, the exchange of goods for goods. Barter's limits, above all the lack of double coincidence of wants, drove the emergence of commodity money, then paper currency, which in most countries became fiat money decreed as legal tender but not convertible into coins or precious metal, then checks payable on demand, and finally the electronic means of payment. Ethiopia's history traces the same path: Axumite coins under Kings Endybis and Aphilas from the third century A.D., then salt bars (amole), cloth and beads, then the Maria Theresa thaler minted in Vienna in 1751 and circulating until 1945, Menelik II's first national coin of 1893, 1933 coins bearing Haileselassie's image, the first paper money of 1914 and the gold-backed notes of 1932, and the birr issued in July 1945.

Functions of money. Money is a medium of exchange, the instrument that pays for goods and services, a lubricant lowering transaction costs and encouraging specialization and the division of labour. It is a unit of account that measures value and makes rational economic calculation possible; without it, a thousand-item shop would need up to 999 exchange ratios on each tag. It is a store of value, holding purchasing power over time, and although stocks, bonds, land and houses also store wealth, money wins on liquidity, the ease and speed of converting an asset into a medium of exchange. It is a standard of deferred payments, letting people buy now and pay later and moving saving from earners to borrowers and investors and into more productive uses.

Demand for money. The old idea tied money demand to the volume of trade, but Keynes' modern view treats the demand for money as liquidity preference, the demand for money to hold, under three motives. The transaction motive holds cash for current payments, through the income motive of consumers who bridge the gap between receiving income and spending it, and the business motive of firms whose cash needs rise with turnover. The precautionary motive holds cash for unforeseen contingencies such as sickness, accidents and unemployment. The speculative motive holds resources liquid to take advantage of future changes in interest rates or bond prices, serving as a store of value for a different purpose.

Supply of money. The supply of money is the sum total of all forms of money held by the community at any given moment, since money must always be held by someone. It consists of metallic money or coins, currency notes, and chequable bank deposits; broadly, currency with the public and deposit money with the public. Currency with the public totals notes in circulation, birr notes and coins, and small coins, minus cash in hand with banks, and the bulk consists of notes issued by the National Bank of Ethiopia. Because most transactions in developing countries are conducted in cash, currency rather than deposits dominates there, and the money supply depends largely on the credit control policies of the banking system.

Money and electronic money. Electronic money is an electronic store of monetary value on a technical device used widely for payments, known also as electronic fund transfer, which uses computers and electronic technology in place of checks and paper transactions and is initiated through cards, codes, PINs, signatures or scans, with ATMs giving 24-hour access to cash. Its advantages are moving money quickly, better record keeping, global transfers and moving large sums without physical burden. Its disadvantages are cybercrime and digital money laundering, the training users need, criminal links to some crypto currencies, and dependence on hardware and software. Electronic money involves many different types of transactions, rights, responsibilities and sometimes fees.

The direct exchange of goods for goods, used before money was invented.
Barter's key requirement that each trader wants exactly what the other offers.
Paper currency decreed as legal tender but not convertible into coins or precious metal.
Medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payments.

workedExamples.problem: A student claims that without money people could easily keep trading, since goods can simply be swapped. Assess the claim using the unit's analysis.
workedExamples.given: Barter requires double coincidence of wants, a common measure of value, divisibility and storable wealth.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: barter is inefficient because each exchange needs a partner with matching wants and a fair ratio of value.
workedExamples.substitution: A farmer trading sheep for wheat cannot find a matching partner easily, cannot settle the ratio and cannot store the wealth safely.
workedExamples.calculation: Each of the five barter limitations raises transaction costs, which is why money replaced barter.
workedExamples.answer: The claim is wrong: barter's limitations, led by the double coincidence of wants, are precisely why money was invented.

workedExamples.problem: A shopkeeper keeps 2,000 birr under the counter for customers' change, another 3,000 birr for a possible price rise next month, and a box of money for medical emergencies. Classify each holding.
workedExamples.given: Three cash balances: for change making, for a future market opportunity, and for emergencies.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: match each purpose to the transaction, precautionary or speculative motive.
workedExamples.substitution: Ready change satisfies current sales; the reserve for price moves is speculative; the medical box is precautionary.
workedExamples.calculation: Planned current payments are transaction, emergencies are precautionary, market-timing balances are speculative.
workedExamples.answer: The 2,000 birr is transaction motive; the box for illness is precautionary; the 3,000 birr for future market movements is speculative.

workedExamples.problem: A cattle trader must pay 40,000 birr for a bull in Bahir Dar, 150 kilometres away, next week. Using the evolution of the payments system, advise the best stage of payments to use.
workedExamples.given: Carrying currency in bulk is easily stolen and expensive to transport.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: each later stage of the payments system reduces transport cost and theft risk.
workedExamples.substitution: Driving with cash exposes the trader to theft and bulk; an account transfer or check moves the sum with a receipt.
workedExamples.calculation: The final stages of the system, banking instruments and electronic transfers, eliminate the physical burden.
workedExamples.answer: Use banking-based payment, a check or electronic transfer, since large sums move cheaply and with records.

workedExamples.problem: A community holds 700 million birr in notes and coins in circulation; banks hold 200 million of it as vault cash; the public also holds 400 million in current account balances. Compute the community's money supply and describe its parts.
workedExamples.given: Currency notes and coins in circulation 700 million; cash in hand with banks 200 million; deposit money 400 million.
workedExamples.formula: Currency with the public = total notes and coins in circulation - cash in hand with banks; money supply = currency with the public + deposit money.
workedExamples.calculation: The currency element is computed first, then the deposit element is added.
workedExamples.answer: Currency with the public is 500 million birr; the money supply is 900 million birr.

commonMistakes: Revising money as only currency, when the definition covers anything generally accepted in payment.
Forgetting that lack of double coincidence of wants is the most important barter problem.
Thinking fiat money is redeemable in precious metal, when by definition it is not convertible.
Matching a saving for illness to the transaction motive; unforeseen contingencies belong to the precautionary motive.
Computing currency with the public without deducting cash in hand with banks.
Calling checks a form of electronic money; checks replaced carried currency but precede the electronic stage.
Listing e-money's disadvantages as theft of notes, when its risks are cybercrime, laundering, training and equipment.
applications: Paying school fees in birr shows the medium of exchange; reading the birr price tag shows the unit of account.
A retailer accepting both cash and a Telebirr transfer handles both the currency element and an electronic store of monetary value.
A household's reserve for hospital visits is composed exactly like Keynes' precautionary motive.
Tracing the 1945 birr explains why earlier generations used amole salt and Maria Theresa thalers.
National Bank of Ethiopia decisions on currency in circulation shape the money supply through credit control.
Deciding how to send a large sum across regions tests which stage of the payments system costs least.
g9-economics-ue6-t6.summary: Unit 6 traced money from definition to digitization: money is anything generally accepted in payment for goods, services and debts, and it replaced barter because barter lacked double coincidence of wants, a common measure of value and workable storage and deferred payments. Money performs four functions, medium of exchange, unit of account, store of value and standard of deferred payments, and people hold it under Keynes' transaction, precautionary and speculative motives, while its supply consists of currency with the public plus deposit money under banking credit control. The payments system evolved from commodity money through paper currency, fiat money, checks and electronic payments, a path Ethiopia walked from Axumite coins and amole salt to the birr, and now to electronic money with its speed and record advantages alongside cybercrime and training costs.

pairs.a: The lack of double coincidence of wants.

Name the two main elements of the money supply.

questions.q: The best definition of money in this unit is anything that is:
options: generally accepted as payment for goods and services
questions.explanation: Money is anything generally accepted in payment for goods or services or debts.

questions.q: Money's most important function is as a medium of exchange to facilitate transactions.
questions.explanation: Without money, all transactions would have to be conducted by barter.

questions.q: When the barter system was replaced by the monetary system, primitive money was first used in the form of:
questions.explanation: Primitive money first took the form of commodity money, such as salt.

questions.q: Explain how the fiat money stage differs from earlier paper currency.
questions.answer: fiat money is not convertible into coins or precious metal|it is legal tender by government decree
questions.explanation: Early paper promised convertibility into coins or metal; fiat money is decreed legal tender and not convertible.

questions.q: A student keeps cash to cover a sudden hospital admission. This holding illustrates the:
questions.explanation: Holding cash for unforeseen contingencies is the precautionary motive.

questions.q: Money held under the speculative motive serves as a store of value, just as money held under the precautionary motive does.
questions.explanation: Both motives store value, but for different purposes.

questions.q: Which institution issues the bulk of the currency notes in Ethiopia?
questions.answer: National Bank of Ethiopia
questions.explanation: The bulk of currency with the public consists of notes issued by the National Bank of Ethiopia.

questions.q: Major drawbacks of paper currency and coins include:
options: being easily stolen and expensive to transport in bulk
lacking a common measure of value
questions.explanation: Paper currency and coins are easily stolen and expensive to transport because of their bulk.

questions.q: Why did salt continue to serve as a medium of exchange in Ethiopia even after the Maria Theresa thaler arrived?
questions.answer: salt had long been popular and generally accepted|it remained one of the popular mediums of exchange
questions.explanation: Salt was the most popular medium until Maria Theresa arrived, and it continued to circulate alongside it.

questions.q: The stage of the payments system that eliminated paperwork by making all payments electronically is:
questions.explanation: EMOP converts completely to electronic telecommunications, eliminating all paperwork.

questions.q: Order these Ethiopian monetary milestones chronologically.
questions.explanation: Axumite coins, Menelik II's coin of 1893, Bank of Abyssinia's paper of 1914, then the birr in 1945.
